title: Your First 90 Days: Turning a New Job Into a Career
excerpt: The offer was the easy part. Here is how to spend your first three months learning before proving, banking small wins, and building allies across teams, so a new job becomes real career momentum.
content:
Adaeze got the offer on a Thursday. An analyst role at a bank in Victoria Island, Lagos, after eight months of applications. She celebrated for one weekend, then walked in on Monday determined to prove she was brilliant. In her first fortnight she corrected a senior colleague in a meeting, proposed a report format nobody had asked for, and stayed late on work that mattered to no one. By month three she was exhausted and her manager had gone quiet on her. She had simply started in the wrong order.

Compare Kwame, who joined an insurance firm in Accra the same month. He spent his first weeks asking questions and writing down the answers. He learned who actually made decisions, which reports leadership genuinely read, and why the claims team didn't trust the sales team. When he finally proposed a fix in his second month, it was small, useful, and aimed at a problem his boss already cared about. By month three, people were inviting him to meetings he had no formal reason to attend.

Same talent, different sequence. Your first 90 days are not about proving you deserved the job. You already got it. They are for converting one offer into something bigger: trust, reputation, and momentum. The stakes are real: the ILO and the African Development Bank estimate that 10 to 12 million young Africans enter the labour market every year, chasing roughly three million formal jobs. A seat at the table is scarce. Here is how to make yours permanent.

The one rule: learn before you prove

Michael Watkins, whose book The First 90 Days is the one managers quote at moments like this, argues that the first task in any transition is to accelerate your learning. New starters rarely fail for lack of skill. They fail by acting on assumptions imported from school or a previous employer before understanding how the new place really works.

So flip your instinct. For the first month, your questions are your work. Every good question you ask early buys you credibility. Every premature opinion spends it.

The 30-60-90 arc at a glance

PhaseFocusSigns you are on track
Days 1 to 30Learn: absorb how the place really works before trying to change itYou can explain your team's goals in your own words, you know who owns what, and your manager has defined what success looks like
Days 31 to 60Contribute: deliver small, visible wins and widen your relationshipsYou have finished at least one piece of work end to end without being chased, and colleagues outside your team know your name
Days 61 to 90Own: take real responsibility and open the career conversationYou own a recurring task outright, your manager assigns work without detailed instructions, and you have asked for and acted on feedback

Days 1 to 30: learn the place, not just the job

You have two jobs in month one. The official one is whatever tasks land on your desk. The real one is drawing three maps. The task map: what your team produces and who consumes it. The people map: who decides, who influences, who has been there fifteen years and knows where everything is buried. The culture map: how people communicate, whether meetings start on time, what gets praised and what gets quietly punished.

Do not assume the company will hand you any of this. Gallup finds that only 12 percent of employees strongly agree their organisation does a great job of onboarding new people. In most workplaces, from a Johannesburg corporate to a ten-person startup in Kigali, the induction is a laptop, a login, and good luck. So onboard yourself. Ask five people for twenty minutes each, with the same three questions: what does this team do well, what frustrates you, and what should someone new here understand quickly? Carry a notebook. Nothing builds early respect like never asking the same question twice.

Then sit with your manager, in week one if you can, and ask the question that shapes everything else: what would have to happen for you to say, six months from now, that hiring me was a great decision? Write the answer down. That sentence is your actual job description.

Days 31 to 60: small wins, wide relationships

Now you contribute, but choose your wins carefully. A good early win is small enough to finish, visible enough to be noticed, and useful to someone with influence. Picture a graduate trainee at a Nairobi logistics firm who makes her name not with a grand strategy idea but by rebuilding a shipment tracker that three teams complain about weekly. Four days of work, months of people mentioning it. Boring problems, solved completely, beat brilliant ideas delivered halfway.

This is also the phase for building relationships beyond your own desk. Your tasks live in one department, but your career will be built across all of them. Have lunch with the finance officer who can explain how budgets actually get approved. Learn the names of the people at reception and the drivers, and greet them properly. In many African workplaces, warmth and respect travel fast, and so does the opposite. These internal allies are the same muscle you will one day use externally: networks surface opportunities long before any job board does, inside companies as much as outside.

Days 61 to 90: from newcomer to owner

By the third month, your goal is simple: own something. A weekly report, a client account, a recurring process that is yours without reminder. Ownership, not activity, is what turns a new hire into a colleague people rely on.

This is also when you ask for feedback instead of waiting for a formal review that may never come. The evidence favours asking: Gallup reports that 80 percent of employees who received meaningful feedback in the past week are fully engaged. Most managers are simply too busy to volunteer it. One question works almost everywhere: what is one thing I should do differently next month? Then do the hardest part. Thank them, act on it visibly, and mention what you changed. Nothing marks you out faster. It is a skill worth sharpening, because how you give, receive, and act on feedback will shape your career more than most technical skills.

Finally, before day 90 closes, open the longer conversation. Ask your manager where this role can grow, what skills the next level demands, and who you should learn from. You are drafting the next chapter, and it belongs inside a career plan flexible enough to survive change rather than in your head.

Mistakes that quietly sink new starters

  • Proving before learning. Big opinions in week two read as arrogance, however right they are.
  • Criticising the old ways. "At my last place we did it better" insults the people who built this one. Ask why things work this way before suggesting another.
  • Staying inside your team. If only five people know you after 90 days, you have a task, not a career.
  • Waiting for feedback. Silence is not approval. Ask early, ask specifically, act visibly.
  • Saying yes to everything. A missed deadline in month two costs more than a polite "I can take that on next week" ever will.
  • Treating anyone as invisible. Receptionists, drivers, cleaners, interns. People notice how you treat people who can do nothing for you.
  • Hiding when you struggle. Asking for help in week six is wisdom. Confessing in week twelve is damage control.

Ninety days is short. Long enough, though, for a workplace to decide what you are: a pair of hands, or a person with a future. Learn first, win small, build wide, ask often. Do that, and the job you fought so hard to get becomes the platform for every job that follows.
